title: Blind Defence Strategy for Canadian Online Poker Players
excerpt: The blinds are the biggest losing seats in poker. Here is how Canadian players should defend them: pot odds, open sizes, 3-betting and out-of-position play.
author: David Andersen
bodyHtml:
Every winning online poker player loses money from the blinds. That is arithmetic, not a leak: you post chips before you see a card, then act first on every street that follows. Good blind defence is therefore not about turning those seats into profit centres. It is about losing less from them than the rest of the field does. For Canadians grinding the Ontario player pools, that gap is often the difference between a modest win rate and a slow bleed.

Why the blinds are the worst seats at the table

Break your results down by seat and the shape is always the same. The button and cutoff print money, middle position breaks even, and the two blinds run deep in the red. That is baked into a structure where you invest blind and then surrender position.

So your goal changes. In the blinds you are playing damage control, and every big blind you save lands on your bottom line. Nobody beats the game from the blinds, but plenty of players lose their entire edge there.

Pot odds and the price you are being offered

In a 0.5/1 game, an opponent opens to 2.5 and the small blind folds. The pot holds 4 and it costs you 1.5 to continue, so you need roughly 27 per cent equity to break even. Against a min-raise to 2 you need about 22 per cent; against a 3x open, about 31 per cent.

Those thresholds are low. Almost any two cards have more than 30 per cent equity against a wide late-position opening range, which is why correct big blind defending frequency is far wider than most small-stakes players believe.

The discount nobody applies

Raw equity is not realised equity. Out of position you get forced off hands that were ahead, you are denied free cards, and your opponent controls the pot size. Treat your equity as worth roughly three-quarters to four-fifths of the calculator number. That discount stops wide defence becoming a licence to call with everything.

How open size, seat and antes reshape blind defence

  • Open size. A min-raise offers a superb price and should be defended very wide. A 3x or larger open should tighten you noticeably, especially with offsuit hands that flop poorly.
  • The raiser's position. An under-the-gun open is genuinely strong and deserves a narrow response. A button open is far wider, so you defend far wider in return. Treating both alike is one of the most expensive habits in low-stakes poker.
  • Antes. Once antes are in play there is more dead money in the middle and your price improves substantially. Ranges widen for everyone, and the blinds become worth fighting for rather than merely protecting.
  • Stack depth. Deeper stacks favour playability. Shorter stacks favour raw card strength, because there are fewer streets in which position can be used against you.

Big blind and small blind are different problems

The big blind

You already have a full blind invested, nobody acts behind you, and the price is the best at the table. That justifies a wide, mostly calling range against late-position opens: all pairs, most suited aces, any suited connection and a slice of offsuit broadways.

The small blind

The small blind is uglier. Only half a blind is invested, so the price is worse. A live player sits behind you and can squeeze. And you are out of position against everyone, with a real chance of playing three-way. All of that argues for defending far more tightly than the big blind, often less than half as often.

Two approaches work. The simpler is three-bet-or-fold: raise your strong hands plus a few suited bluffs, and fold the rest. The advanced version adds a small flat-calling range against late-position opens when the big blind behind you is passive. Both beat calling too wide and then guessing on the flop.

Three-betting versus flat-calling

Three-betting solves your positional problem by ending the hand early. The best candidates either dominate the calling range, such as strong aces and big pairs, or carry blockers and postflop equity, such as suited aces and connectors. Weak offsuit hands make poor three-bets: they fold out everything they beat.

Flat-calling keeps weaker holdings in your opponent's range, which is what you want with medium-strength and speculative hands. The real mistake is having no three-betting range at all. If you only ever raise aces and kings, opponents open wider and barrel relentlessly, and your blind defence collapses into flop folds. Surviving the flop out of position

Defending preflop is worthless if you hand the pot over on the flop. Opponents continuation bet small, often a quarter to a third of the pot, precisely because it forces you to defend wide for a cheap price. Against those sizings, fold rarely: bottom pair, gutshots, backdoor flush draws and overcards with a backdoor straight are all fine continues.

Check-raising is your main counterweight: it takes back the initiative and puts your opponent in the uncomfortable seat for once. Build that range from strong made hands and genuine draws on boards that favour your calling range, such as low connected textures. Dry ace-high flops belong to the raiser, so check-call and move on. Correct flop calls are often clear folds once a second barrel arrives.

Multiway pots and squeeze spots

When a raise is called before the action reaches you, everything tightens. Equity splits more ways, speculative hands lose value because someone will usually have connected, and bluffing gets less profitable. Favour holdings that make nutted, easy-to-play combinations.

The exception is the squeeze. A late-position open followed by one or two flat calls signals weakness, and a well-sized three-bet from the blinds can win a large pot uncontested. Use it selectively, size it larger than usual, and pick hands with blockers.

Adjusting to loose-passive online games

Small-stakes pools, including plenty of tables in Ontario's regulated market, are looser and more passive than theory assumes. Opponents open too many hands, three-bet rarely, continuation bet automatically and then give up on the turn. Defend the big blind wider than a solver would, float more flops with backdoor equity, and check-raise turns after a check-back.

Also weigh aggression by street: in a passive pool a river raise usually does mean strength, but a flop bet often means nothing at all. If you are choosing where to put in volume, our 888poker Ontario review and our Canadian poker room reviews compare traffic and table quality.

Common blind defence leaks

  • Over-defending trash. Wide is not infinite. Offsuit nine-four flops nothing playable and costs you money every time curiosity wins.
  • Folding too much to min-raises. A min-raise gives you the best price in poker. Folding two live cards there is a plain error.
  • Auto-folding the small blind. Tight is correct, but folding every hand makes you free money for anyone watching from the button.
  • Never check-raising. A defender who only check-calls can be barrelled off the pot forever.
  • Treating every opener alike. One hand can be a clear call against a button steal and a clear fold against an early-position raise.

Cash games versus tournaments

In cash games stacks stay deep and survival carries no bonus, so the pot-odds logic above applies cleanly. In tournaments, antes improve your price, shorter stacks push you towards three-bet shoving rather than flat-calling, and pay jumps near a bubble can make folding a marginally profitable call correct. The bottom line

Know your price, discount it for being out of position, widen against small opens and late-position raisers, tighten hard in the small blind, and keep a real check-raising range. None of this makes the blinds profitable. It makes them cost less, and over a long grind that is where a win rate comes from.
